"We're seeing only the early stages of it," Ford observed. "But this is a country of a couple of million people that, perhaps against most people's expectations, hosted and put on an outstandingly well-organized World Cup."

"So, in many ways, they've proven that they can execute on a plan, and I think you know they're very likely to continue to make inroads into the industry in the next few years."

articles.title: 'Ramayana' Doubled Visitors at Kerala's Jatayu Rock, Official Says as India Pitches Itself to Global Productions at WAVES Film Bazaar
articles.summary: Nitesh Tiwari's "Ramayana" has doubled visitor numbers at Kerala's Jatayu Earth's Center, known locally as Jatayu Rock, Ministry of Tourism joint secretary Harikishore S. told a WAVES Film Bazaar panel in Goa, where Indian officials pitched a single-window filming portal and state incentives to international producers. The site is traditionally held to be where the […]
articles.content:
Filming " Ramayana " at Kerala's Jatayu Earth's Center, known locally as Jatayu Rock, doubled visitor numbers at the site, Ministry of Tourism joint secretary Harikishore S. told a WAVES Film Bazaar panel in Goa, where Indian officials pitched a single-window filming portal and state incentives to international producers.

Producers on the same stage said crew skill and speed give India an edge, though Sunita Ram of Rasika Pictures warned the country still lacks the studio space to keep its biggest shoots at home. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories How to Watch the CMA Awards (And Taylor Swift's Performance) Live Online How 'Law & Order: SVU' Pulled Off the Impossible With Latest Milestone: 'It Will Never Happen Again'

The session, "Filming in India: India's Rise as a Global Production Hub," featured Prithul Kumar, joint secretary, broadcasting, at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting; Harikishore; Alan McAlex, founder of Suitable Pictures ("Santosh," "Sister Midnight"); and Ram, whose Rasika Pictures handles service production and co-productions ("A Suitable Boy," "120 Bahadur").

Kumar said the India Cine Hub portal first went live at Film Bazaar on Nov. 21, 2015. At the time, it mainly handled film visas and permissions for foreign productions. In 2023, the ministry widened its scope after concluding that overseas producers also needed support on the ground and a way to find local resources. The portal now combines permission applications with directories of crew, equipment and services, an interactive location map, and information on state and central incentives.

State governments, local administrations and central agencies including the Railways, the Archaeological Survey of India and the civil aviation authorities, which clear drone use, all sit behind the single window. Each state has a nodal officer who follows up on permissions in person, Kumar said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"It's a hundred times more difficult than manufacturing or assembling a product because every step is a new one, and the filmmakers actually have to turn dreams into reality," Kumar said of filmmaking.

He clarified that the portal is a permissions tool rather than a networking one; collaboration between filmmakers and service providers happens on the separate WAVES Bazaar market platform. Kumar also said the Ministry of Tourism has signed a non-binding, non-commercial MoU with production houses including Netflix, Amazon and JioCinema to encourage more content about India, such as its food, rivers and forests, and to encourage them to shoot in a wider range of places.

Kumar also asked filmmakers in the room to list themselves on India Cine Hub so producers anywhere in the world can find them.

Harikishore said roughly 80% of what a producer needs comes from the states, with the central ministry handling the other 20%. He pointed to Madhya Pradesh, which he said pays back up to 75% of the cost of a film shot in the state. "And it is not a policy paper; they have given it to 50 people in the last two years," Harikishore said.

He said the jump in visitors at the site is set to last. In his view, what holds other locations back is a knowledge gap among state decision-makers about what productions actually want, and he proposed workshops in which producers brief officials. Kumar agreed, noting that states tend to upload only tourist landscapes to the portal. "Shooting happens in a village, it happens in a house," Kumar said. The ministry has also asked states to pick 10 locations from past hit films and brand them, he added, citing Bekal Fort, where a song from "Bombay" was shot. Kumar said Jatayu Rock should likewise carry "Ramayana" branding.

McAlex said India used to draw productions mainly when scripts had Indian stories or characters. "We had projects coming in to shoot American interiors because the actors had a very short window, so they didn't have to go back to the U.S.," McAlex said. He added that AI and volume stages are now opening the door to exterior work too, and that local crews and VFX facilities let productions keep everything in one place.

As examples of Indian crews pulling off complex work, he cited a British Film Institute-funded project whose executives doubted a mid-day company move in Mumbai could be done. His team managed it. He also pointed to an American production on which only the director and DP flew in, and an all-Indian crew pulled off a stunt sequence on a fifth floor. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Ram said international producers are now confident that Indian working standards match those of the U.K., Europe and the U.S., and that they no longer need to fly in large teams when they can mix in local crew. "Every day of shoot is like, you know, launching a rocket every day. But that's world over, not just India," Ram said. She tells anyone who doubts what's possible in India that 24 hours there can equal three weeks of work elsewhere, because "we can turn things around here faster than anywhere else."

Ram added that she looks for new locations with every script. One recent project set in Mumbai ended up shooting in the small town of Karaikudi instead. "They'd never even heard of it, but it's something you introduce, you know, with every film," she said.

WAVES Film Bazaar is the market component of the International Film Festival of India .

articles.title: 5 TV Shows That Took Over Pop Culture, But Nobody Talks About Anymore
articles.summary: Remember when it felt impossible to go a week without hearing someone talk about a specific show? Sometimes, an unexpected TV craze takes over, and a series becomes so popular that it seems like the entire world can't stop talking about it. There have been several examples of this over the years. But at some […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Remember when it felt impossible to go a week without hearing someone talk about a specific show? Sometimes, an unexpected TV craze takes over, and a series becomes so popular that it seems like the entire world can't stop talking about it. There have been several examples of this over the years. But at some point, that success starts to fade, whether because the show has ended or because its seasons failed to live up to its potential . And even though some fans are still around, they aren't really talked about anymore.

These are shows that had a massive impact when they were at their peak. Can you think of any? We've selected 5 that you've certainly watched or at least heard about, and that were once some of the main talking points in pop culture.

Stranger Things hasn't been gone for that long, but given how huge its peak was, when the internet seemed to stop everything to watch the show and even crashed Netflix , it deserves a spot on this list. The iconic series follows a group of kids and teenagers who have to deal with supernatural events after Will Byers (Noah Schnapp) mysteriously disappears, leading everyone to discover a parallel dimension and secret government experiments. It's a mix of sci-fi and horror, with plenty of '80s references, and it caused a huge frenzy for almost a decade. It launched its cast into stardom, brought Dungeons & Dragons back into the spotlight, and sent Kate Bush's "Running Up That Hill" to the top of the music charts.

And naturally, hype eventually dies down. However, in this case, it feels like people got oversaturated with it. Even after spin-offs were announced and Stranger Things: Tales from '85 was released, people didn't seem to keep thinking about it. The truth is that all the controversy surrounding the writing, especially in the final season , played a part in that, since even though fans kept watching until the end, the reactions were more negative than positive. The show is still a pop culture landmark, of course, but it's curious how nobody seems really eager to talk about it anymore. Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure was recently announced and got some attention, but we'll have to wait and see whether it can come anywhere close to the original show's level of buzz.

Here's a show that may not have reached a massive global audience, but it became an unexpected hit in 2023. And once people found out it was based on a book by Taylor Jenkins Reid, copies started flying off the shelves. Daisy Jones & The Six won audiences over by telling the story of a fictional '70s rock band, from its rise to fame to its breakup, with a special focus on the toxic relationship between lead singer Daisy Jones (Riley Keough) and musician Billy Dunne (Sam Claflin). But what really generated buzz was the collective effort to make the band feel real: the actors learned to play instruments, recorded the songs, and took part in a promotional campaign that made it seem as though the group could have actually been successful back in the day.

The album Aurora , created specifically for the series, topped the iTunes album charts, and plenty of fans took to social media to express how much they wanted the cast to go on tour . However, even though the production turned into a huge sensation, the hype only lasted a few months. And to be honest, the reason has a lot to do with its format: Daisy Jones & The Six is a miniseries with a pretty conclusive ending, so it's difficult to come up with a convincing way to continue the story . Much of its success came from the fun of following a band that felt real, and by the final episode, the only real open door involved the relationship between the two main characters. So, in the end, there wasn't much to keep people engaged.

Glee took the TV world by storm in the 2010s, so much so that it's even getting a reboot now. And even though it's been quite a while, anyone who was keeping up with the most popular shows back then, whether they watched it or not, knows this musical series. Basically, it became a big deal because it knew how to connect with its audience. The story follows the members of New Directions, a school choir made up of students who use music to deal with the challenges of high school, from relationships and bullying to issues of identity and acceptance. It was a clever concept, as people could relate to the characters while also enjoying covers of hit songs in every episode. And to give an idea, many of those covers made it onto the music charts, and the cast even went on two concert tours.

And apart from the music, the show has a lot of humor and drama, with a light tone that still allowed it to tackle subjects other series often avoided at the time. Unfortunately, though, Glee became a victim of its own formula: by the later seasons, much of the original cast had left the series , and the constant musical numbers and storylines became tiring for pretty much everyone. Still, it remained a talking point for quite some time, not only because of its plots but also because of the controversies and behind-the-scenes news with the cast. But one positive thing we can take away from its success is that many of the musical shows we see today owe something to the path it helped pave.

When you think of groundbreaking series , Lost definitely has to be on the list ( although its finale is a whole different story ), since it defined the kind of storytelling that gets viewers coming up with endless theories and debating every little detail with other fans. It follows the survivors of a plane crash who find themselves stranded on an island, where they discover some mysterious phenomena, strange structures, and secrets. And a big part of its appeal was the way it revealed new clues and details about the characters—who could forget The Numbers, the hatch, or the Others? Every new episode had something to talk about, especially since streaming wasn't a thing back then and people had to wait a whole week for the next chapter.

But maintaining that level of audience engagement was bound to come with some risks eventually. So, after six seasons, the show ended with a highly divisive finale, as everyone had spent years following the mysteries and were expecting clear answers. Much like what happened with Stranger Things and Game of Thrones , the excitement with Lost lost some of its momentum because of the way its story wrapped up. You can still find people who look back on it, but it's not exactly the kind of series they are as eager to recommend as they once were. It was a defining show, with a legacy that influenced several productions that came after it , but it has also become something of a ghost in pop culture, and bringing it up can still be a sensitive subject.

Some people might argue that The Vampire Diaries doesn't really belong on this list, since it's still relatively easy to find people talking about the show compared to some of the others here. Still, it was very much the product of a passing craze. There was a time when the vampire genre was everywhere, and the series arrived right in the middle of that trend. Based on L.J. Smith's books, the story follows Elena Gilbert (Nina Dobrev), a young woman who meets Stefan Salvatore (Paul Wesley) and soon finds herself caught in a love triangle with him and his brother, Damon (Ian Somerhalder), two vampires with totally different personalities. It's a pretty familiar genre setup, but the story starts expanding to include witches, werewolves, supernatural families, and many plot twists .

Overall, the series showed up at exactly the right time, with basically everything audiences were looking for after the success of Twilight . Eventually, the cast became some of the most popular faces on TV, and the spin-offs The Originals and Legacies came along . However, its ratings started to decline in the later seasons because of some storytelling issues, and also due to the whole vampire craze dying down. So, while you might still come across people talking about The Vampire Diaries today, it's usually in the context of nostalgic TV shows more than anything else.

articles.title: There's A Reason Ross Isn’t In One Of The Biggest Friends Scenes (But It Did Lead To A Good Joke)
articles.summary: He got there eventually!
articles.content:
Given that the core premise of Friends centered on the friendships between Monica, Rachel, Phoebe, Ross, Chandler and Joey, it makes sense that many of the iconic sitcom's biggest moments would feature all six characters together. However, there was one huge event that didn't include David Schwimmer 's character, and there's a specific reason why. While Ross's absence from this particular scene was unfortunate, it did lead to a clever joke and a nod to something the character had become notorious for.

Monica and Chandler's romantic engagement scene is topped off by Joey, Phoebe and Rachel coming in to celebrate with them. The only person absent was Ross. No, David Schwimmer and Friends weren't "on a break," he was just busy overseas when the engagement scene was filmed.

As Friends co-creator David Crane pointed out on the DVD commentary, all of David Schwimmer's scenes for the two-part Season 6 finale had to be filmed in the first week because the actor was in England filming Band of Brothers for HBO . Crane spoke about having to film the scene without Schwimmer, saying:

While all of the drama between Monica and Chandler was going on throughout "The One with the Proposal," Ross was busy breaking up with college student Elizabeth (a cliffhanger involving her revealing she's pregnant was discussed for the season finale , but ultimately scrapped). From what it sounds like, that was all filmed during the first week of production for these final episodes. The grand finale involving Chandler and Monica wasn't filmed until later.

As you'll recall, as the gang is celebrating with a group hug, Phoebe points out that "Ross isn't here!" to which Rachel responds, "Oh, hell, he's done this three times. He knows what it's about!" It's a funny way to acknowledge and then dismiss Ross's absence from his sister and best friend's engagement, while also firing a shot at Ross's "three-divorce guy" reputation. As Crane put it, that was the silver lining to the situation, after debating whether or not to point out the lack of Ross in the scene:

I'll admit, the absence of a main character due to the actor being involved in another project might bother me under other circumstances, but it's hard to complain here. Band of Brothers is its own kind of epic, after all. Stephen Spielberg and Tom Hanks ' HBO miniseries – based on Stephen Ambrose's non-fiction book about a parachute infantry company serving in World War II – won several Emmys and has been widely remembered and appreciated in the decades since its release. What's more, Schwimmer's portrayal of Captain Herbert Sobel is easily one of his most memorable roles outside of the hit sitcom.

The writers made the best of the situation by working in the joke about marriage proposals being old hat for Ross.

The sequel to " Bandit Queen ," the 1994 drama about Indian outlaw Phoolan Devi, is aiming for a release at the end of 2027 or early 2028, producer Bobby Bedi tells Variety , with the screenplay now in its final draft and casting underway.

Bedi, who produced Shekhar Kapur's original, is calling the follow-up "Bandit Queen MP." Honey Trehan , director of the Diljit Dosanjh-starrer " Satluj ," was unveiled as director earlier this month. The new film picks up where Kapur's ended, following Devi from her years in prison to her assassination, and a little beyond. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"The film is really about the tumultuous love story of a married man and a prisoner negotiating their lives in this 'even more dangerous' landscape through freedom, fame and fortune. But to what end?" Bedi says.

He adds that women's role in politics is back at the forefront, and that Devi was a soldier for the cause in her day.

"My first film was about the rape and revenge and fate of a lower caste woman in India's rural landscape. This film happens to be the story of the political power and ultimate fate of a low caste woman in the urban political landscape. It just happens to be the same woman," he says.

Bedi describes the project as new territory for both him and Trehan.

Trehan worked on Bedi's 2003 production "Maqbool," directed by Vishal Bhardwaj, and the producer says the maturity of his later independent work stood out. "And then came 'Satluj,' earlier called 'Punjab '95.' It blew me over. Well researched, superbly cast, well directed. Very impressive. He is clearly a perfectionist," Bedi says. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Satluj," in which Dosanjh plays human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra, spent nearly four years in India's certification process. Originally titled "Ghallughara," it was cleared by the Central Board of Film Certification with 21 cuts and an enforced title change to "Punjab '95," and was pulled from the gala slot it had been set for at the 2023 Toronto International Film Festival. The film finally premiered uncut on ZEE5 Global on July 3 this year. Less than two days later, ZEE5 took it down in India, saying it would be "unavailable in India until further notice." Days after that, the platform removed it from its international catalogue as well.

Trehan says "Bandit Queen" inspired filmmakers of his generation, and that being asked by Bedi to carry its legacy forward is special. He is currently absorbed in the material and the research Bedi has already done, and has known the producer since his Delhi theater days, before "Maqbool."

"He is such a hands-on producer," Trehan says.

Phoolan Devi's story has already returned to the screen this year with Richie Mehta's "Phoolan," from Amazon MGM Studios and Namah Pictures, which premiered at the Toronto Film Festival. articles.title: BBC Being Investigated Over Antisemitism By Government Adviser

The UK government's antisemitism tsar is probing the BBC .

John Mann told the Today programme that he has opened up an investigation to see how "widespread" Jewish staff's "feeling of discomfort" is within the corporation. According to The Times, whistleblowers have already told him they consider the BBC a "hostile environment."

Mann said his investigation should complete by Easter before he reports back to the broadcaster. He invited "anybody who is Jewish inside the BBC past and present with something to say" to come forward and speak with him. Related Stories News Huw Edwards To Speak On TV For First Time About Criminal Actions & Fall From Grace In Channel 4 Doc News Richard Hammond Says He Was Approached By BBC About 'Top Gear' Return

On Today, he said he had already heard from employees who had read about the investigation in The Times just three hours prior. Rather than listeners or viewers, he said the probe concerns "the lived experience of Jewish staff past and present at the BBC," and will "report facts, not opinions." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

Deadline understands the BBC has not yet been notified about Mann's investigation. Mann has been the UK government's adviser on antisemitism for seven years.

In the wake of October 7 , antisemitism has been an issue the BBC has struggled to get to grips with. At times, this has spilled out in the open. Last month, one of the exec producers behind Oscar-winner Mr. Nobody Against Putin was reported to have settled with the BBC for £400,000 ($523,000) over antisemitism claims, although an internal BBC investigation did not uphold her complaint. "I think I made too much noise about being a Jew inside the BBC," Lucie Kon told The Telegraph a few weeks ago.

A BBC spokeswoman said: "We take any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC. We have introduced compulsory training on antisemitism for all our staff and we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have. We are determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted.”

articles.content:
Former " Top Gear " host Richard Hammond has revealed that he was approached about returning to the BBC 's revived version of the car show, but declined because he's "too old."

The presenter appeared on Times Radio on Wednesday to discuss the series, shortly after it was announced that Gordon Ramsay would be taking the wheel as host. Hammond co-hosted "Top Gear" alongside Jeremy Clarkson and James May from 2002 to 2015. Related Stories Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree' Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed to Saturday Due to Storm

"I did talk to [the BBC] about 'Top Gear' relaunching, and I'm sure they went to the others as well," Hammond said. "They came to me, you know, was I interested? And no, I'm too old. I think it needs a younger cast." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Asked why he turned down the idea, Hammond said: "No, I've done it. I wouldn't want to revisit it. Well that was our 'Top Gear,' wasn't it? We did it, the three of us. And when we left and went on together, it was the three of us. But that was our show."

As for his thoughts on Ramsay hosting the program — who, at 60, is four years older than Hammond — he seemed open-minded.

"Will Gordon work? Well, TV chefs all love three things: cooking, obviously, massive watches and cars. In his case, four, swearing as well," Hammond said. "But they all love cars, so I don't doubt his passion his there. So let's see what he does with it."

Ramsay is an avid car lover who has his racing license and has previously appeared on "Top Gear" as a guest. Following a four-year hiatus after co-host Andrew Flintoff was badly injured in a crash, the show is set to film next year "across the U.K. and around the world," according to a press release, and is eyeing a 2028 launch. Racing driver The Stig is set to return, though it is yet to be announced if Ramsay will have any co-hosts. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Hammond concluded his thoughts on the new "Top Gear" by saying that he sees plenty of crossover between food and cars.

"I've long wanted to make a TV show, actually, where I pair up with a chef and we talk about cars and cooking," he said. "Because there is a big tie-in between them as subject strands, there's a big connection … So I think [Ramsay] will bring the right audience to it, but I'll be interested to see what they do with it."

Variety has reached out to the BBC for comment.

articles.title: The Ghostbusters Fight the Macy's Day Parade in Their Forgotten Thanksgiving Episode
articles.summary: Most cartoons treat Thanksgiving as a way to teach kids to be grateful for what they have in life. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Most cartoons treat Thanksgiving as a way to teach kids to be grateful for what they have in life. It's a great lesson but one that's as stale as those unseasoned dinner rolls from a can that nobody wants to eat but does so the family member who made it isn't offended. The Real Ghostbusters Thanksgiving episode, on the other hand, treats the day like a spooky superbowl, culminating in a clash between two ectoplasmic behemoths that rival Godzilla's battles with King Ghidorah . We're talking about "The Revenge of Murray the Mantis" from 1987, and its main event is a smackdown with two titans ready to make a statement.

The episode's bad guy is an homage to the oversized radioactive bugs from so many classic 1950's monster movies. In particular, this atomic age antagonist harkens back to The Deadly Mantis from 1957, a fairly forgotten movie in its own right with dated effects, but a concept that is a perfect fit for the whimsical and often eerie world of The Real Ghostbusters . Who better to battle this monster than another huge part of the Ghostbusters world — and we do mean huge — than the Staypuft Marshmallow Man. This episode is full of throwbacks to nostalgia, but it goes deeper than its characters and hits another explosive moment from the original film that had lasting effects on the franchise.

"The Revenge of Murray the Mantis" was part of The Real Ghostbusters second season of syndication, and according to writer Richard Mueller was directly inspired by the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade that runs from the Upper West Side of Manhattan through Midtown. The story begins on the eve before the holiday, as the Ghostbusters finish work on adjustments to their containment unit that includes a brand new airlock (which is never seen or used again) so Egon can use it to become the first ambassador of the spirit world. Meanwhile, a crew of workers are inflating a balloon for their Thanksgiving parade, which is revealed to be on the grounds of what used to be the city morgue. A phantom mist rises from the ground and enters a float, possessing it ahead of the next day's event.

While the Ghostbusters enjoy their time in the ECTO-1 as part of the parade, things go awry when the balloon of beloved cartoon character Murray the Mantis loses control. Venkman blasts it, revealing a meaner insect within that's as tall as a skyscraper. It wreaks havoc on the city, forcing the team to summon their secret weapon from within the containment unit — the Staypuft Marshmallow Man. "The Big Guy" is released and meets his clawed rival uptown for a kaiju-sized showdown in Central Park, leading to a knockdown brawl that ends in Murray's destruction. The Ghostbusters are heralded as heroes, while Staypuft enjoys his time floating overhead above the crowd as a makeshift replacement float for Murray.

After Staypuft's victory in this episode, "The Big Guy" returned again throughout the series in various appearances. Some were cameos in the background or hearing its name mentioned in passing, but episodes like "Cry Uncle" and "Sticky Business" utilized the possessed snack monster to its full potential. The latter explained how Staypuft came under the employment of the Ghostbusters, with Egon positively charging a sample of the marshmallow goo to make it a friendly giant instead of a fiendish bad guy. Most recently, Staypuft was brought back into the cinematic universe by appearing in mini-form in Ghostbusters: Afterlife and its sequel Frozen Empire . These mischievous micro-mallows acted more like Gremlins, getting into trouble on a smaller scale instead of smashing public property and stepping on churches.

Besides referencing Gozer earlier in the episode and bringing Staypuft back into the fold, there's another nod to the original Ivan Reitman-directed film that kicks off the story's third act. As mentioned earlier, Ray and Egon's modifications to the containment unit become a critical part of the plot while later acting as a catalyst to Staypuft's return. After the phantom mantis appears for the first time, the NYPD comes knocking on the firehouse doors with an arrest warrant for the Ghosbusters. After barging in through an unlocked door, two patrolmen enter the basement and drag Egon away from the ectoplasmic storage facility, but not before the scientist sets his plan into motion.

As the Ghostbusters are lined up outside to be arrested, the front doors of their headquarters burst open with a strong gust of spectral winds as the sidewalk begins to quake. A swell of energy crumbles the firehouse roof, leading to a psychokinetic explosion as the containment unit releases an unnatural disaster of spooky proportions. This is a direct throwback to the containment unit explosion from the first film, where Walter Peck demanded it be shut down, resulting in releasing every single ghost they had captured earlier through the movie (though most weren't shown on camera). In this instance, only Staypuft was let loose, but the way the cartoon showed this happening as well as the inspiration for it was clearly an homage to the 1984 classic.

This explosive moment wasn't the only time The Real Ghostbusters made a reference to the movie. Most notably, "Citizen Ghost" from the first season told the story that connected the cinematic universe into the animated one by explaining what happened immediately after Gozer was sent packing by a total protonic reversal, showing us why the team transitioned from matching khakis into colorful jumpsuits and how Slimer joined the team. Scenes from the film were briefly shown in "Take Two," another episode from the same season where the GB's head to Hollywood to work on a movie about themselves. After taking down the obligatory ghost du jour, the team watch the premiere of their movie which uses footage from the live-action version.

Do you remember this episode of The Real Ghostbusters , and will you make it part of your Thanksgiving tradition? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Indie Filmmakers at WAVES Film Bazaar Look to 'Dangal' China Playbook, Pop-Up Cinemas and Screening Fees to Find Audiences
articles.summary: Aranya Sahay, the director of "Humans in the Loop," is working with Prasad Shetty, the distributor who released "Dangal" in China, as he plans how his second feature, "Mayapuri," can reach audiences in India, China and the U.S. Sahay outlined the plan at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market of the International Film Festival of India […]
articles.content:
Aranya Sahay, the director of "Humans in the Loop," is working with Prasad Shetty, the distributor who released " Dangal " in China, as he plans how his second feature, "Mayapuri," can reach audiences in India, China and the U.S.

Sahay outlined the plan at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa during "After the Applause: Can Independent Cinema Find Its Audience?," a panel moderated by critic and curator Meenakshi Shedde. Filmmakers and producers from India, Nepal, Ghana and Russia shared what happens after the festival applause dies down. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories NBC Celebrates 100th Anniversary With Amy Poehler, Jimmy Fallon and More Stars at Rainbow Room Soirée Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate

"Dangal" earned more in China than in India, Sahay said. The film grossed nearly $193 million there. Shetty asked local stars to post about it. Its run grew from roughly 100 shows to about 20,000. Sahay traced its success to a story about a father who comes to see his daughter's potential, which struck a chord with Chinese fathers of only daughters raised under the one-child policy.

"Can tapping into these markets cross a threshold of say 50 million, say 70 million? And if that happens, then it's not just a one-off, it's not just one film – it becomes an inlet for other Indian films to have a release in the U.S.," Sahay said. In the U.S., he added, the team is partnering with a company he hopes will help them hit that number.

Sahay's first feature found its audience the slow way. "Humans in the Loop" follows an Adivasi woman in a remote part of India who takes a data-labeling job training AI. Its premiere at the Mumbai Film Festival (MAMI) cost it the chance of a world premiere at a bigger international festival. But Sahay noticed that about a third of the audience at his Mumbai screenings went on to write personal essays about the film on Instagram, so he kept screening it wherever he could, including at the India International Centre and Bangalore International Centre. Before each show he contacted 40 journalists. Around 10 would turn up and three would write. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The film later won the Grand Jury Prize at the Indian Film Festival of Los Angeles and landed a Sloan Foundation distribution grant. Nearly 100 community screenings in India and the U.S. built enough momentum to bring Kiran Rao aboard as executive producer, and Netflix later released the film worldwide.

Sahay is also partnering with Ahmedabad university MICA on a grant-cum-fellowship and post-production support program for seven filmmakers from marginalized communities, with one project picked from Film Bazaar's Work-in-Progress Lab. The support includes 350 hours of sound design and 100 hours of color grading, worth INR2 million–INR2.5 million ($21,000–$26,000). He also pointed filmmakers to platform Humans of Cinema, which has given an upfront INR4 million ($42,000) grant without taking a stake.

Tribeny Rai, whose Indo-South Korean co-production "Shape of Momo" premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, said the film did better in India's big cities than in the northeastern states when it was released theatrically. She recently screened it for 3,000 students in her home state of Sikkim.

"I don't think there is a lack of audience; I think there's a lack of a bridge where they can access our films," Rai said.

Darjeeling filmmaker Anmol Gurung is launching an initiative called the Indian Nepali Film Market, which plans to build 100 community theaters in areas where Nepali-speaking people live, Rai said. Building an audience from scratch with every release is "a toxic cycle," she said, adding that filmmakers can start such efforts but can't stand in for infrastructure.

"Even film festivals don't pay screening fees, you know? It's crazy because they have curators who are paid, they have a venue that is paid, but as soon as we ask for screening fees they are like, 'But you know, we are putting you up there.' I don't want to be up there, I want money." Rai said. She and a few other filmmakers from India's Northeast no longer hand over their films without a fee.

Abinash Bikram Shah, whose " Elephants in the Fog " won the Jury Prize in Cannes' Un Certain Regard section and is Nepal's Oscar submission, said he added a hint of thriller to the film to draw a wider local crowd. Released in September through Popcorn Films, it ran for six weeks in Nepal despite devastating floods at the time, and did well in France, where his producer and a distributor co-released it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Shah now plans to screen the film in the village where it was shot, on a big screen in front of the forest, and to work with LGBTI rights NGO Blue Diamond Society, where star Pushpa Singh Lama works, on screenings across Nepal. A screening in Janakpur, in Nepal's southern belt, is also underway. After a win at New York LGBTQ festival NewFest, the team held an impact screening for diplomats at the UN House in New York, and plans one in London. Lama recently won best actress at the Asia Pacific Screen Awards.

Ghanaian American director Amartei Armar, whose debut "Our Time Will Come" won two prizes at Locarno and is playing at IFFI, said Ghana has one or two traditional cinemas with a combined capacity of around 200 seats. Tickets cost 100–150 cedis ($10–$12), while many Ghanaians earn 600–800 cedis a month. He and his producer are setting up a company to bring back the mobile cinemas Ghana had in the 1960s and open distribution routes for Ghanaian, African and Global South filmmakers.

Armar recalled that Indian and Korean soaps dubbed into Twi became so popular in Ghana that viewers petitioned the government to fly in the Indian actors, then were stunned to find they couldn't speak the language. When Shedde suggested AI dubbing could widen his reach, Armar said: "I would rather have that than the AI making the films for us!"

Russian producer Katerina Mikhaylova, founder and CEO of Moscow-based Vega Film, said she now focuses on commercial, audience-oriented films and maps out target markets at script stage rather than in post-production. She is currently shooting Indian-Russian co-production "Cow: Journey to Love," a story in the vein of "Eat Pray Love" and "Bridget Jones" that she said any woman could relate to, with a core audience aged 25 to 40.

From the audience, Yusuf Shaikh said the CineNow Fund, launched at the event a day earlier, will back prints and advertising for independent films and take them to small towns, using pop-up screens in community and town halls.

Rai's production company, Dalley Khorsani Productions, takes its name from a chili found in Sikkim. "It has a very peculiar aftertaste after you eat it. So I just want our films to leave that aftertaste," she said.

“Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean : The Immersive Adventure,” the upcoming theatrical adaptation of the hit Johnny Depp movie, is getting ready to set sail.

The production, which is due to open in London early next year, has now shared behind-the-scenes rehearsal footage as the cast practice their sword fighting and rig-climbing skills.

Directed by Olivier-winner Matt Costain, the show sees George Maguire step into the iconic boots of Captain Jack Sparrow opposite Phil Daniels (“Quadrophenia”) as Captain Barbossa, Lily Blunsom as Elizabeth Swann, Harrison Wilde as Will Turner and Gleanne Purcell-Brown as Anamaria. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’ Director James Gray Calls Out ‘Dumb, Ethically, Morally Bankrupt’ Festival Competitions and Quips That He’s Giving Up on Cannes: ‘I’ve Learned My Lesson’ Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support

The production is set to launch on March 10, with previews from Feb.16, at Secret Cinema’s new flagship venue in Greenwich Peninsula, just a stone’s throw from where the films were shot. It is currently due to run through June 6.

“We’ve taken everything Secret Cinema does best and pushed it further than ever before, creating a new kind of theatrical experience where the story doesn’t just happen in front of you – it happens all around you,” said Merritt Baer, Secret Cinema’s artistic director and producer and president and co-founder of TodayTix Group. “This is exactly the kind of show we’ve been building towards and opening it in our new home at Greenwich Peninsula makes it even more exciting.”

Richard Hammond has revealed that the BBC sounded him out about getting back behind the Top Gear wheel for the show's upcoming reboot.

The presenter said he declined the opportunity to return to the motoring show he helped turn into a global phenomenon alongside Jeremy Clarkson and James May .

Hammond disclosed the BBC's approach during an interview with Times Radio on the day that Gordon Ramsay was unveiled as the new host of Top Gear.

"I did talk to them about Top Gear relaunching, and I'm sure they went to the others as well. They came to me, and [asked] was I interested? 'No, I'm too old,' [I responded]," Hammond said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); } Related Stories News Gordon Ramsay To Host Revived 'Top Gear' For BBC News BBC Journalists Vote To Take Strike Action Over Job Cuts

"I've done it. I wouldn't want to revisit it. That was our Top Gear , wasn't it? We did it, the three of us, and when we left and went on together, it was the three of us. But that was our show.

"The BBC owns Top Gear and has had it for decades, and I think right now should be making a show that actually tells us what's happening in the world of cars."

Times Radio presenter Kait Borsay asked Hammond if he would be interested if Clarkson and May returned to Top Gear.

"We've done it. Let somebody else. We made our show in the way we did, and for our time," he replied. "The BBC should be making a TV show that tells us, the consumers: This is what's happening in the world of transport."

Hammond hosted Top Gear between 2002 and 2015, before leaving the BBC with Clarkson and May and launching The Grand Tour on Amazon Prime Video.

Ramsay was announced as the next host of Top Gear four years after Andrew Flintoff’s crash. Ramsay will lead the series alongside a soon-to-be-announced lineup of co-presenters, with The Stig returning.

Filming will take place across the UK and around the world in 2027, with the Top Gear test track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home.

Ramsay said: "At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected – surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.”

Iron Man, Captain America, Thor, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Black Panther — all of […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Since 2008, the MCU has broken a lot of cinematic ground. The franchise pioneered the modern shared universe , creating an interconnected series of live-action superhero stories that has brought to life characters no fan ever thought they’d see onscreen. Iron Man, Captain America, Thor, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Black Panther — all of whom were relatively unknown to casual moviegoers — became box office champions. And as a result, the Marvel brand has expanded its reach by leaps and bounds, earning the fandom of people who have never picked up a comic book before. And with Avengers: Doomsday coming, that potential is even greater.

The upcoming film reunites directors Joe and Anthony Russo with their Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame stars Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans, all of whom are taking center stage in the MCU for the first time in seven years. Given the box office records and fan acclaim its two predecessors earned, Avengers: Doomsday certainly has a lot to live up to. In this case, it also has to win back MCU doubters who may have wavered during the divisive Multiverse Saga run. But even before the film hits theaters, it is already continuing the MCU tradition of breaking boundaries.

For much of its run, the MCU seemed committed to an unspoken “three-and-done” policy. No matter how successful the film and how much it made at the box office, each individual branch of the greater tapestry that is the MCU ended after three films, at least for a while. Downey only headlined three Iron Man films, Evans starred in three Captain America movies, and likewise, the Guardians of the Galaxy and Ant-Man films appear to remain trilogies. The Avengers movies always seemed like the exception to this rule, which makes sense since the heroic line-up shifts from film to film. So when Marvel announced its third and fourth Avengers movies — initially revealed as Avengers: Infinity Wars, Parts One and Two — no one batted an eye.

And now Avengers: Doomsday promises to extend Earth Mightiest Heroes’ cinematic run. By all accounts, in fact, the story will directly address the team’s absence over the past few years, which allows the opportunity for some fun meta-commentary. But it also marks the first five-film run in the MCU. And if we’re to take the original X-Men films and the First Class run as separate franchises within Fox’s X-Men universe, then the Avengers series stands as the first live-action superhero franchise to get five movies deep. Even on the DC side of things, Superman and Batman capped off at four, with Superman IV: The Quest for Peace and Batman and Robin .

In that respect, Avengers: Doomsday marks a milestone for the MCU and superhero cinema as a whole, an accomplishment that will only be furthered by next year’s Avengers: Secret Wars . However, fans shouldn’t expect Marvel to begin building out its heroes’ movie series to four, five, or six installments. The only obvious holdover is Tom Holland's Spider-Man series, which — as a Sony and Marvel co-production — was always going to be an anomaly anyway. True, the MCU has been toying with going beyond its unspoken trilogy rule in recent years, with Thor: Love and Thunder and Captain America: Brave New World both hitting theaters during the Multiverse Saga.

But the dismal reception to the fourth Thor movie will likely give Marvel pause before it greenlights a fifth installment, assuming Chris Hemsworth’s God of Thunder makes it out of Avengers: Doomsday alive, that is. And with Sam Wilson taking over the mantle of Captain America, Brave New World technically counts as the start of a new trilogy focused on a different hero. In any case, while Anthony Mackie would love to star in more Captain America movies , that seems far from a sure thing right now. Instead, Marvel seems intent on course-correcting following Secret Wars . So it’s telling that X-Men , Black Panther 3 , and Ghost Rider are among the only confirmed films for Phase 7 and beyond right now.

Which MCU heroes’ solo franchises would you like to see continue beyond three films? Sound off in the comments section!

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18, 2026.
